issues.legal_issue: The power to regulate house accommodation in cantonment areas includes regulation of privately owned and occupied premises and the landlord-tenant relationship, including rent control and eviction.
material_facts: The premises were privately owned and let to a tenant, and were situated within a cantonment area.
The tenant obtained a fair-rent determination under a state tenancy law, and the owner later sought eviction.
The challenge concerned whether the power to regulate cantonment housing was limited to accommodation needed or used for military purposes.
issues.conclusion: The power to regulate house accommodation in cantonment areas extends to all such accommodation, whether privately owned or occupied, and includes control of rents, termination of tenancies and eviction; it is not confined to accommodation required or used for military purposes.
issues.legal_principle: Entry 3 of List I of the Seventh Schedule gives Parliament power to regulate house accommodation throughout cantonment areas. The Court read regulation broadly to include who may occupy accommodation, the terms and duration of occupation, rent and eviction. It relied on Prout v. Hunter, Property Holding Company Ltd. v. Clark, and Curl v. Angelo to explain that rent-control legislation’s purposes include protection against both excessive rent and eviction; it also considered the history of cantonment house-accommodation legislation.

predicates.constitutional_scope_dispute: The proceeding concerns the scope of legislative authority over housing in a cantonment area.
predicates.dwelling_in_cantonment: The premises subject to the dispute are situated within a cantonment area.

issues.definition: When a constitutional scope dispute concerns privately let premises in a cantonment and rent or eviction regulation, parliamentary regulation extends to the tenancy and eviction.

issues.legal_issue: A state legislature cannot regulate the landlord-tenant relationship for house accommodation in cantonment areas where that subject falls within Parliament’s exclusive legislative authority.
material_facts: The premises were situated in a cantonment area and were occupied by a tenant under a private letting.
A state tenancy law had been extended to the cantonment area, and the tenant relied on its protections.
The owner challenged the validity of that extension on the ground that regulation of cantonment housing was within Parliament’s legislative field.
The High Court held the extension notification invalid, and the appeal challenged that decision.
issues.conclusion: Parliament has exclusive authority to legislate on the landlord-tenant relationship insofar as it concerns house accommodation in cantonment areas; the state law’s extension to the cantonment area was ultra vires and void, and the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 246, Parliament’s exclusive authority over matters in List I prevails over state legislative powers, including powers associated with land and landlord-tenant relations under Entry 18 of List II and transfer of property and contracts under Entries 6 and 7 of List III, insofar as they concern cantonment housing. The Court approved Nawal Mal v. Nathu Lal and disapproved A.C. Patel v. Vishwanath Chada, F.E. Darukhanawalla v. Khemchand Lalchand, Kewalchand v. Dashrathlal, and Babu Jagtanand v. Sri Satyanarayanji and Lakshmiji.
